topics.title: TCP Flow Control, Congestion Control and the Socket API
topics.description: Two windows and two signals. A sender may have in flight at most min(rwnd, cwnd), and the smaller one names the limit: rwnd is a 16-bit byte count in every ACK (at most 65535, scaled by an option), cwnd is inferred from loss and never transmitted. Flow control is a budget - usable = rwnd minus bytes in flight, so 6 MSS advertised with 2 unacknowledged leaves 4, and on a lossless 100 ms path the 16-bit ceiling alone caps the rate at 5.24 Mbps. Congestion control is a curve: slow start adds one MSS per ACK and therefore doubles per round trip until ssthresh, then congestion avoidance adds one per round trip; a timeout sets ssthresh to half the flight and cwnd to 1, three duplicate ACKs set cwnd to the threshold under Reno. The page walks four real traces in code - GATE 2014 Set 1 Q27 (16 MSS at a timeout, threshold 8, eleven round trips, 1100 ms), GATE 2020 Q55 (ten round trips, 2 to 32 KB by doubling then 44 KB, with rwnd 50 KB never binding), GATE 2024 Set 2 Q54 (12 MSS, threshold 6, 4 MSS after a timeout against 8 after duplicate ACKs) and the 2018 Q14 statement set - then turns the sawtooth into 0.75 x W_max / RTT (21.9 Mbps at 100 MSS of 1460 B over 40 ms) and the path into a bandwidth-delay product of 1.25 MB that needs a scale factor of 32. The socket API closes the clause: socket, bind, listen, accept on the server, socket and connect on the client, MSS = MTU - 40, and TIME_WAIT for the active closer. The page runs 57 checks on its own model - the min-window identity, every growth step, the threshold cap, both loss signals, the sawtooth average, the scale factor and the segment arithmetic - and reports them under the canvas.

topics.title: IP Fragmentation, CIDR and NAT
topics.description: Three arithmetics on one idea: where does a bit, or a byte, sit inside a longer string, and who may rewrite it. A prefix is a cut, so a /27 has block size 32, and 200.10.11.144/27 runs from .128 to .159, which makes .158 the last assignable host (GATE 2015 Set 3 Q38). A routing table is read by longest prefix match and never by first match: 200.150.68.118 matches /16, /19 and /24 but not the /27 that ends at .95, so interface 3 answers (GATE 2023 Q55), and on the 2024 Set 1 table two of five hosts take R2 for 40 packets. Two equal blocks merge only when they are adjacent and aligned, so GATE 2022 Q45 aggregates to 164.0/22 with 168.0/22 and covers 2048 addresses with nothing extra. Fragmentation is the same arithmetic in bytes: budget is MTU minus header, the usable payload is that budget rounded down to eight, and the offset is the running sum over eight - 1000 bytes into a 100-byte link gives 13 fragments (2016 Set 1), 7488 UDP bytes give six with a 116-byte last fragment (2025 Set 2), and 1420 bytes over links of 542 then 360 give six at the receiver with offsets that stay absolute (2024 Set 1). NAT rewrites the source outbound and the destination inbound, with the header checksum recomputed and the total length untouched (2024 Set 1 Q21). The page runs 41 checks on its own model - block boundaries, candidate lists, aggregation cover, and five fragmentation invariants on every list - and reports them under the canvas.

topics.title: Lexical Analysis, Parsing and Syntax-Directed Translation
aliases: lexical analysis parsing and syntax directed translation
topics.description: One question at four objects: how much future may a parser look at before it decides? The scanner decides with none beyond the current token, so it is a finite automaton and the longest match is its only rule - twelve tokens from twenty-six characters, with the wrong split drawn beside the right one. FIRST and FOLLOW are least fixed points, printed pass by pass on the GATE 2012 grammar, and FOLLOW is re-derived a second way by expanding sentential forms, so the two methods check each other. A cell holding two productions is the definition of not LL(1), not a slip - and on that grammar the cell for a does hold two. The LR(0) collection for S to CC is built by closure and goto in seven states, and the same automaton under three reduce policies gives SLR two conflicts on the GATE 2025 Set 2 grammar, LALR none, and canonical LR(1) ten states against seven on S to CC. On the GATE 2026 Set 2 grammar the LR(0) ACTION table has five shift-reduce conflicts and SLR has none on the identical automaton. Associativity is read off the recursion side and precedence off the grammar's depth, with both trees built by the page from the GATE 2014 Set 2 grammar. Syntax-directed translation is run for real: the GATE 2016 scheme prints 231 in reduce order, three-address code is emitted and executed on a tiny VM against direct evaluation, and the GATE 2022 scheme evaluates to 80. 44 checks run on load and the pass count is printed under the canvas.

topics.title: Context-Free Grammars and Pushdown Automata
aliases: pumping lemma for context free languages
topics.description: One question at four scales: how many independent comparisons does the language demand? The stack hands back the reverse of what it stored, so a mirror and a count can be checked and a copy cannot - which is why ww^R is three rules and ww is not context-free at all. The page counts parse trees rather than derivation orders (2 for i+i*i, 5 for i+i*i+i, the Catalan numbers) and shows the levelled grammar cutting them to 1 with the language unchanged. It converts eight grammars to Chomsky normal form in code and checks on every string up to length five that no string changed sides, then runs CYK on the result. A traced run of aabb pushes, pops and closes with an epsilon move, and the machine is checked against the definition on all 127 strings up to length six. Every legal split of a^2b^2c^2 and a^3b^3c^3 is enumerated and none survives, as are 51 splits for the copy language and 716 for w a^n w^R b^n, which is GATE 2019 option C. GATE 2017 Set 1's union and intersection, 2009's odd-palindrome grammar, 2011's DPDA-versus-NPDA pair and 2022's statement cluster are each recomputed rather than quoted. 55 checks run on load and the pass count is printed under the canvas.

topics.title: Distance Vector and Link State Routing
topics.description: Two families, one question: what may a router know? Distance vector is the Bellman-Ford equation run locally - add your link cost to each neighbour's claim and keep the minimum - so the cost and the next hop fall out of the same computation. Its disease is provenance: nothing records where a number came from, so a dead route climbs 2, 3, 4 ... 16 and only RIP's ceiling of 16 stops it, which is also why a RIP path is at most 15 hops. Split horizon removes the two-router loop and not the three-router one, and the page simulates both. Link state floods each router's own links until every router holds the same map, then runs Dijkstra from itself, which is why its trees differ while its databases do not. GATE CSE 2011 Q52 and Q53 are recomputed round by round (3,2,0,2,5 and then 10, where the true distance is 9 - one round is not convergence), 2021 Set 2 Q45 gives 8 via Y and 7 via X, 2022 is 0.5, and the RIP/OSPF facts come from RFC 2453 and RFC 2328. The page runs 60 checks on its own model, including both algorithms against an independent all-pairs computation on four graphs, and reports them under the canvas.

topics.title: Link Layer: Error Detection, MAC and Ethernet
topics.description: Three jobs, one question: what can a receiver conclude from bits that may be wrong, and what can several stations conclude from a wire they must share? A CRC is division - append r zeros, divide modulo 2, send the remainder - and its guarantees come from the generator's algebra: every burst up to the degree, every odd-weight error only when x+1 divides it, which is why 1011 (three ones) misses an odd pattern that the model exhibits while 1001 catches all 4096. Detection is a parity question and correction is a distance question, so d_min >= s+1 and d_min >= 2t+1 are different answers to different questions, and a Hamming syndrome names the bit until two bits flip and it names an innocent one. Sharing is the vulnerable period: 2T without listening, T with slots, one propagation delay with carrier sense, one round trip with detection - which forces L >= 2 tau R and makes GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q6 come out at 20000 km/s. GATE CSE 2017 Set 1 Q32 is remainder 101, 2021 Set 2 Q34 is 100, 2017 Set 2 Q34 is d_min 3 correcting 1, 2018 Q55 is 50 metres because those nodes never detect. The page runs 50 checks on its own model and reports them under the canvas.

topics.title: Transactions and Concurrency Control
aliases: active partially committed committed failed aborted
topics.description: One test, applied five times: find the conflicts, turn each into an edge, ask whether the edges can all hold. The precedence graph answers conflict serialisability and names the serial order - GATE 2014 Set 3 has S1 acyclic with the unique order T2, T3, T1 while S2 carries both T1->T2 and T2->T1, and GATE 2022's order is T1, T3, T4, T2. Enumeration, not a formula, gives GATE 2017 Set 2's 54: 70 interleavings of the two four-operation transactions, one of them the serial T1-before-T2 and 53 equivalent to T2 before T1. Conflict serialisability is sufficient and not necessary - the blind-write schedule r1(A) w2(A) w1(A) w3(A) has a cycle and is still view equivalent to T1, T2, T3. Recoverable, cascadeless and strict are a one-way ladder read off commit positions, and GATE 2014's S1 is conflict serialisable yet no two-phase-locking execution can produce it, because T1 needs X across positions 0 to 8 while T3 needs it at position 2. The page runs 40 checks on its own model and reports them under the canvas.

topics.title: File Organisation and Indexing (B and B+ Trees)
aliases: file organization indexing b and b+ trees
topics.description: Two computations and one structure. A node is a block, so the order is a floor of a byte ratio: 8p + 12(p-1) <= 1024 gives 51 pointers and the 50 keys GATE 2015 Set 3 keys, and 16n + 6 <= 1024 gives the 63 leaf entries of GATE 2007 where forgetting one chain pointer gives 64. Occupancy is order arithmetic: maximum 5 keys means order 6, so the minimum is 2 and not the 3 of GATE 2010. Cost is counted in blocks: GATE 2020 needs 205 and 204 to reach three levels and four accesses including the record, and the GATE 2015 Set 2 index fetches five nodes for 7 <= key < 15 because 13 still needs the last leaf. Every tree drawn is built by this page's own insertion and deletion code, and 39 checks re-validate it after every operation.

topics.title: Regular Expressions and Finite Automata
aliases: counting strings in a regular language
language is a set of strings
topics.description: One question asked four ways: how much of the input must the machine remember? The obvious machine for (a+b)*b(a+b) remembers the last two symbols and needs 7 states, and table filling reduces it to the 4 that GATE 2017 Set 1 keys; a 4-state NFA has 16 subsets of which only 4 are reachable, which is why the 2^n bound of GATE 2018 is a ceiling and not a floor; 'divisible by 2 but not by 3' is one counter modulo 6 with residues 2 and 4 accepting, not residue 0, because zero is divisible by both; a product modulo 7 needs 6 states because only the six nonzero residues are reachable; 'ends with 011' and 'contains 011' both cost 4 states and differ only on the witness 0110; Thompson builds (a|b)*abb in 14 states and accepts exactly the strings ending abb across 511 checks; elimination recovers (0 + 10*1)* from the two-state even-count machine; and a^p b^p cannot be pumped for any split. Every count is computed by the page and checked against the machine's own defining properties.

topics.title: Functional Dependencies, Normal Forms and Decomposition
topics.description: One procedure, four operations: closure, keys, minimal cover, and the two decomposition tests. The closure of AB grows to ABCDE in three passes on the GATE 2022 schema and 8 superkeys fall out of 32 subsets; the four schemas of GATE 2018 Q42 land on four different rungs because Schema II's email -> rollno has a prime right side and Schema IV's courseid -> credit does not; GATE 2004 studentPerformance stops at 3NF for the same one-clause reason; GATE 2001's AB | CD split keeps both dependencies and turns two rows into four, which is what lossy actually means; and GATE 2001 Q2.23 has no decomposition that is BCNF, lossless and dependency preserving at once, which the model confirms by testing all 14 partitions of ABCD. Every verdict is computed by the page, not quoted from a key.

topics.title: Relational Algebra, Tuple Calculus and SQL
topics.description: One set of tuples, three notations: the six primitive operators on the eighteen-tuple CR instance from GATE 2017, projection collapsing 18 tuples to 4 while SQL's SELECT keeps all 18, the natural join's degree as a sum minus the common attributes, division as a double difference giving 4 rows (SA, SC, SD, SF) with SB and SE each one course short, GATE 2022's four spellings of "owns all the brands" where options C and D each die on a different witness, a shared calculus variable becoming R.Q = S.X in GATE 2026 Set 1 Q43 (option B), the clause order FROM-WHERE-GROUP BY-HAVING-SELECT-ORDER BY, NULL as a third truth value so that x = 5 and x <> 5 return 1 row each of 3 and NOT IN over a NULL returns nothing while NOT EXISTS returns 2, AVG dividing by the 3 non-NULL salaries, and an ER design mapping to six relations.

topics.title: Disk Scheduling (I/O Scheduling)
topics.description: Why a 100-cylinder seek costs 10 ms while a rotation costs 4.17 and a transfer 0.04, so the only decision left is the order; FCFS at 640 cylinders against SSTF at 236 on the same eight requests, and why nearest-first is greedy but not optimal (139 against 118); SCAN going to the physical end for 331 while LOOK turns at the last request for 299, and the 16 cylinders of travel that serve nothing; C-SCAN's 382 made of 146 plus a 199-cylinder jump plus 37, and C-LOOK jumping to the lowest request instead of to cylinder 0; GATE 2016's C-LOOK at 346 where the jump alone is 181, GATE 2015's 130 against 140 with the key at 10, GATE 2014's request at the head costing nothing but changing the order, GATE 2020's false statement, and GATE 2018's 200 cylinders and 3 reversals coming to 85 mW.

topics.title: File Systems
aliases: number of blocks to hold free block numbers
insert a block in the middle
topics.description: Why a file is three tables in three places and one open costs three reads; contiguous against linked against indexed on the same eight-block file, and why only two of them avoid external fragmentation; the FAT costing 400,000 bytes of a 100-million-byte disk, and a 4-byte pointer leaving 65,532 usable bytes and 65,468 wasted; an inode's 12 direct plus single plus double pointers reaching 1,049,612 blocks and 4.0 GB, and 8 plus 16 plus 256 blocks being 35 KB and not 280; one insertion costing 101 accesses contiguous against 52 linked, summing to 153; a 32 MB bitmap for a 1 TB disk and 16,417 free-list blocks from 511 entries each; six block reads for one path and the two directory operations that must scan everything; the link count walking 2 to 1 to 0 while a symbolic link points at a path instead; and the last block, the pointer and the inode table as the only three things ever wasted.

topics.title: Memory Management and Virtual Memory
topics.description: Why five holes place four requests under best-fit and only three under first-fit; the offset bits that are never translated; 2^20 entries of 4 bytes as 4 MB; the split that keeps each table inside one page; a hit path and a miss path averaged to 122 ms; six steps of a page fault and 30 ns from one fault per million; FIFO, LRU and optimal simulated cell by cell; nine faults becoming ten when a frame is added; and 2000 pages costing between 3 and 1025 table pages.

topics.title: Synchronisation and Deadlock
topics.description: Why an assignment is three steps and an interleaving can lose one; the three requirements and the state that breaks progress; Peterson counted over 34 states; a semaphore as a permit counter whose negative value is a queue; the bounded-buffer wait order that deadlocks; monitors and condition variables; the four Coffman conditions; a cycle that is not a deadlock; and Banker's safety check with the n(K-1)+1 <= m bound.

topics.title: Processes, Threads and IPC
topics.description: Why a process is an address space plus an execution context plus a PCB, and a program is none of those; the six legal state edges and the two that never exist; a context switch as pure overhead with the fraction s/(q+s); fork as one call with two returns, and the doubling that turns n calls into 2^n processes and 2^n - 1 children; the shared and private columns of a thread, and why a thread switch skips the page table; user-level against kernel-level threads; and the IPC mechanisms separated by what they carry and who may use them.

topics.title: I/O Interface, Interrupts and DMA
topics.description: Why a device is not a memory and needs three registers on the bus; how memory-mapped and isolated I/O name those registers at two different prices; why polling has no separate overhead because the CPU never leaves the loop; the five interrupt events in their one legal order and why the save precedes the jump; the two jobs hidden in interrupt handling, naming the source and ranking the sources; the DMA controller's registers and its request/grant handshake; burst, cycle stealing and transparent as three schedules; and the four formulas that turn a clock rate, a register width and a device rate into a number.

topics.title: Memory Interfacing and Interleaving
topics.description: Why a memory chip is a rectangle and the memory you need is a bigger one, so covering it takes two independent divisions; how the address becomes a bit budget split between what a chip needs and what a decoder needs; how a chip-select condition turns into an address range; how a decoder is counted by its tree rather than by its chips; and how m slow banks behind one bus turn a sequential stream into parallel work — with the condition that licenses the overlap formula, and a counterexample for when it does not.

topics.title: Instruction Set and Addressing Modes
topics.description: Why an instruction word is a bit budget that must be spent exactly, how a variable-length opcode is built from one reserved escape code and why it must be prefix-free, how one expression costs 3, 5, 7 or 8 instructions depending on how many addresses each instruction may name, how eight addressing modes turn one machine state into eight effective addresses, what each mode costs in memory reads, and why a branch stores a signed distance from the next instruction rather than an address.

topics.title: Hashing: Hash Functions and Collision Resolution
topics.description: Why collisions cannot be avoided, and what to do instead: chaining against probing, the load factor, linear probing's clustering, the primality and coprimality conditions that make a probe walk cover the table, deletion with tombstones, and the four expected-probe formulas with the load factors where each breaks down.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming: Formulation, Tables and Classic Problems
aliases: divide and conquer versus dynamic programming
topics.description: Why a recurrence with repeating subproblems needs a table: the state, the transition, the base case and the fill order, executed on knapsack, LCS, matrix chain, LIS and Floyd-Warshall, with the one loop direction that silently turns 0/1 knapsack into the unbounded problem.

topics.title: First-Order Logic
topics.description: Why a predicate waits for a value, why for-all is a big AND and there-exists a big OR, why the domain changes the answer, how NOT flips a quantifier, and why the order of two different quantifiers decides who may depend on whom.

topics.title: Propositional Logic
topics.description: What counts as a proposition, the five connectives built column by column, why an implication is true when its hypothesis is false, which rearrangement of it is equivalent, and how to refute an argument form with one row.

topics.title: C Fundamentals: Types, Operators and Control Flow
topics.description: Why a type is a promise and not a size, how the spelling of a literal already fixes its type, why a char is lifted to int before arithmetic, why -1 < 1u is false, which overflows the standard defines and which it does not, and how loops and switch decide what actually runs.

topics.title: Pointers in C
topics.description: What an address is, how dereferencing works, why pointer arithmetic scales by element size, how an array decays to a pointer, and the four traps GATE builds questions on.

topics.title: Sets and Set Operations
topics.description: Why membership is the only primitive, why the empty set is not the set holding zero, why subset is an implication so the empty set is inside everything, why a power set has 2^n elements, and how the union, the product and the subset-pair count are all one counting argument.

topics.title: Relations and Their Properties
topics.description: Why a relation is only a set of pairs, how the diagonal and the mirror pairs decide all six properties at a glance, why antisymmetric is not the negation of symmetric, the one-cell counterexample to "symmetric plus transitive gives reflexive", how a closure is the smallest repair of one named property, and how equivalence relations and partitions are the same object counted twice.

topics.title: Functions and Their Properties
topics.description: Why a function is a relation with two promises, why the codomain is declared and the range is computed, how to read injective and surjective off the columns of the matrix, when the three properties collapse into one, the four counts, and which properties survive composition and set operations.

topics.title: Partial Orders, Hasse Diagrams and Lattices
topics.description: Why an order needs three promises and antisymmetry is the one usually missing, how to strip an order down to its covers and read it back by walking upward, why maximal is not greatest and a bound is not a maximum, how one pair without a join stops a poset being a lattice, and why two complements are enough to prove a lattice is not distributive.

topics.title: Counting and Combinatorics
topics.description: Why every count is a sum of disjoint alternatives or a product of independent stages, how two yes/no questions sort a problem into one of four boxes, why every division is an apology for over-counting, how identical objects are counted by where the separators go, why inclusion and exclusion is forced by the alternating signs, and why a pigeonhole guarantee is always one more than the largest arrangement that avoids the condition.

topics.title: Recurrence Relations
topics.description: Why a recurrence is a rule plus base cases, how to build one by conditioning on the last symbol, how unrolling turns a first-order recurrence into a sum, why the largest characteristic root can contribute nothing, why a repeated root costs an n, how dividing out an exponential collapses a recurrence, and why the master theorem is silent in the gap between its cases.

topics.title: Graphs: Connectivity and Structure
aliases: number of edges in a tree
topics.description: Why the degree sum is twice the edge count, why a tree on n vertices has exactly n - 1 edges, why every connected graph contains a spanning tree, how a cut vertex differs from a bridge, why connectivity is bounded by kappa <= lambda <= delta, why bipartite is the same as no odd cycle, and why Euler has a degree test while Hamilton has none.

topics.title: Graphs: Matching and Colouring
topics.description: Why a matching is a set of edges and a colouring a partition of vertices, why maximal is not maximum, how one augmenting path proves Berge's theorem, why Hall's condition is exact, why Konig's equality needs bipartiteness, and why the chromatic number is trapped between a clique and delta plus one.

topics.title: Monoids and Groups
topics.description: Why a rule on a set is a complete table, how the five promises stack into semigroup, monoid, group and abelian group, why (Z6, x) is a monoid and (Z6, +) a group, how the order of an element is counted, why a cyclic group has one subgroup per divisor, and why A4 stops Lagrange running backwards.

topics.title: Generating Functions
topics.description: Why a sequence becomes one series, the five atoms that answer every paper question, how a product of series is a product rule of counting, why the denominator is the recurrence, and why a quadratic has two solutions but only one generating function.

topics.title: Boolean Algebra and Minimisation
topics.description: Why a Boolean function is its truth table and an expression is only one description of it; the identities and why duality halves them; minterms, maxterms and the two canonical forms; the map's Gray-code labels, wrapping edges and power-of-two blocks; don't-cares as optional ones that can never make an implicant essential; prime implicants against a cover; product-of-sums by grouping the zeros; and the tabular Quine–McCluskey method that scales past four variables.

topics.title: Number Representation and Arithmetic
topics.description: Why a bit pattern means nothing until you name its representation, how the three signed encodings differ by one wasted zero, why two's complement is a wheel with one self-negating pattern, why carry and overflow answer different questions, and how IEEE 754 spends 32 bits on a sign, a biased exponent and an implied-1 fraction.

topics.title: Functions, Scope, Lifetime and the Preprocessor
topics.description: Why a parameter is a copy and a swap changes nothing, why an array parameter is really a pointer, why a name and an object have separate lives, what static and extern do to duration and linkage, and why a fully parenthesised macro still evaluates its argument twice.

topics.title: Recursion
topics.description: Why a recursion needs a reachable base case, how four frames push for sumTo(3) and unwind to 6, why calls and peak depth are different numbers, what a tail call does and does not promise in C, and how to answer a value question and a cost question about the same call tree.

topics.title: Arrays, Stacks and Queues
topics.description: Why an index is a multiplication and not a lookup, how row-major and column-major decide which index moves, what C does not check, why a stack needs exactly one index and a queue needs two, which output orders one stack can produce, and why a circular queue's full and empty states collide.

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.description: Why a node stores the address of the next one instead of computing it, how two assignments in the right order splice a list and two in the wrong order lose it, why a by-value head cannot report a new first node, what a doubly linked prev pointer buys (O(1) deletion), why a circular list with one rear pointer makes both queue operations constant, and how reversal and cycle detection are counted.

topics.title: Trees, Binary Search Trees and Heaps
topics.description: Why a tree is a shape and a search tree is a promise: the four traversals and which pairs rebuild a tree, the subtree order that a parent-only test misses, Catalan counting of shapes and search trees, deletion by the inorder successor, and the two heap promises that let an array hold a tree with no pointers.

topics.title: Asymptotic Complexity and Recurrences
topics.description: Why a running time is a function and not a stopwatch, how O, Omega and Theta differ by which inequality is promised, how a witness pair proves a bound and a table of values cannot, the nine-rung growth ladder and the ratio test that replaces guessing, the pair of functions that is neither O nor Omega of the other, the three cases as three functions, and the recursion tree whose level sums give the master theorem and its gap.

topics.title: Binary Search and Its Variants
topics.description: One loop and six different tests: the invariant that makes it correct, the exact count floor(log2 n) + 1 including the final comparison, the two loop shapes with the stall and the 32-bit overflow, first and last occurrence among duplicates, rotated arrays, bitonic arrays, search on a monotone predicate, and the decision tree that explains why log n cannot be beaten.

topics.title: Sorting Algorithms and the Comparison Lower Bound
topics.description: Why a sort makes two promises and not one, the three quadratic sorts with their real comparison counts, the decision-tree wall at log2(n!) that no comparison sort can pass, merge sort and quicksort and heapsort read off their structures, how counting and radix sort step outside the wall, and why stability and in-place are two separate questions.

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms: Choice, Exchange and Counterexample
topics.description: Why a greedy algorithm is a claim about a criterion rather than a technique, what the greedy-choice property buys you that optimal substructure does not, how an exchange argument is written in four moves, and the two counterexamples that show where greed fails.

topics.title: Graph Algorithms: Traversals, MSTs and Shortest Paths
aliases: level order traversal of a graph
topics.description: Why a BFS tree records fewest-edges distance and a DFS tree does not, how the cut and cycle properties license Kruskal and Prim, how to count minimum spanning trees by collapsing forced edges, and why one negative edge makes Dijkstra report 2 where the answer is 1.

topics.title: Combinational Circuits: Adders, Multiplexers and Decoders
topics.description: Why a combinational circuit is its truth table, how a half adder becomes a full adder and a full adder becomes a chain whose carry costs two gate levels per column, why look-ahead turns that ripple into a formula that is constant depth with wide gates and logarithmic with two-input gates, how one adder subtracts by complementing and adding one, how a multiplexer is a lookup table and a decoder is all the minterms at once, and why two adjacent ones covered by different terms make a correct expression glitch.

topics.title: Sequential Circuits: Latches, Flip-Flops, Counters and Machines
topics.description: Why a loop of two gates is a memory, why the SR latch has a hole and what its release does, why a latch is transparent and a flip-flop samples once, why a level-triggered JK toggles many times while the clock is high, how setup and hold bound the clock frequency differently, how ripple and synchronous counters differ by a factor of n, how a ring counter gives n states and a Johnson counter 2n, and how an FSM design is finished only when the unused encodings are checked.

topics.title: ALU and Control Unit Design: Datapath, Hardwired and Microprogrammed Control
aliases: alu data path and control unit
topics.description: Why the ALU is a multiplexer over gates that compute at once, why k functions need ceil(log2 k) select lines, why carry and overflow are different questions, why one bus means one transfer per step, and how hardwired and microprogrammed control trade speed for flexibility — with every width and every count computed and checked.

topics.title: Pipelining and Hazards
topics.description: Why a pipeline does not make an instruction faster, how the slowest stage plus one latch sets the beat, why k + n - 1 is the cycle count, and how structural, data and control hazards each add their own correction — with the load-use stall that survives every forwarding network.

topics.title: Memory Hierarchy and Cache
topics.description: Why a small fast memory helps at all, how the address is cut into offset, index and tag, the three mappings, the exchange of index bits for tag bits, a simulated LRU walk, the three Cs by counterfactual, write policy, and the move from a miss rate to a CPI.

topics.title: CPU Scheduling
topics.description: The one decision a CPU scheduler makes, and the five numbers that score it: turnaround C - A, waiting T - B, response first - A, utilisation and throughput. FCFS and the convoy effect (8.25 average waiting on a fixed set); non-preemptive SJF at 7.5 with its exchange-argument proof and the known-burst assumption it needs; SRTF at 6.0 and the 16 units its longest job pays; round robin at 10.75 waiting but 3.75 response, with both degenerate quanta; preemptive against non-preemptive priority, starvation and aging; multilevel feedback queues with demotion and promotion; and the fraction q/(q+s) that decides how small a quantum can be.

topics.title: Layering, Switching and Performance Metrics
topics.description: Four problems, four layers, one narrow interface: a message grows a header on the way down and loses one on the way up, and only the link header is rewritten at each router. Then one arithmetic, asked three ways - a circuit pays a setup and no per-hop packet time, one packet pays a transmission and a propagation term per link, and P packets over N links pay N+P-1 transmission terms because the links overlap. GATE CSE 2012 Q44 is 1005 ms, GATE 2022 Q59 is 7.08 ms, GATE 2024 CS1 Q36 is 8.008 s, and GATE CSE 2014 Set 2 comes out T1 = T3 > T2 because the repeated headers cancel the pipelining gain.

topics.title: Turing Machines and Undecidability
topics.description: One question at three objects: does a run end, does a language have a machine that always ends, and can any machine answer that for every machine. The page runs a tape interpreter on seven machines, traces 0 to the n 1 to the n through fourteen configurations on 0011, and checks six of them against their definitions on all 63 strings of length at most 5. It builds a universal machine and confirms it reproduces every machine on every input of length at most 3. Then the counting: 31 strings of length at most 4 give 2 to the 31 languages against 31 descriptions, and a six-by-six accept matrix whose flipped diagonal is checked to differ from all six rows. The halting construction is executed, not quoted: the machine N built from a decider disagrees with it on N's own description in both cases, while the same decider is correct on all seven ordinary machines. The wrapper that turns halting into emptiness is built for six machine/input pairs and checked on both lines, and Rice's witnesses are two machines this page actually runs. The boundary is tested too: the k-step decision procedure with k = 6 agrees with a brute-force search over inputs up to length 10, which is why GATE 2020 Q26, 2021 Set 1 Q39, 2016 Set 2 Q44 and 2022 Q46 have a decidable option at all. Two recognisers are dovetailed and decide all 31 strings of length at most 4 in 14 rounds, which is Post's theorem computed rather than stated. 43 checks run on load and the pass count is printed under the canvas.
